title: Central, CO Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Central wells have a 277-foot median depth, with finished well costs modeled at $24,000-$39,700.
h1: Central, Colorado Well and Drilling Guide
intro_html:
Buying mountain property near Central means understanding fractured-bedrock wells before you commit to a lot, house plan, or offer. Records within the mapped area show a median well depth of 277 feet, a median reported yield of 7.0 gallons per minute, and a median static water level 69 feet below the surface.

Those figures are useful for planning, but they are not a guarantee for a specific parcel. Rock fractures can change sharply over short distances. Neighboring well permits, the intended use, access for a drill rig, and the location of septic improvements all matter.

sections.heading: Central well depths reflect fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
Central sits in mountain terrain where permitted wells are primarily associated with unnamed fractured-bedrock formations. Fractured granite and gneiss do not hold or transmit water evenly, so depth can vary substantially between nearby lots. The median completed depth is 277 feet, while the middle half runs from 160 to 405 feet.

For a drilling bid, that spread matters more than the median alone. A contractor planning around the median may still need to price a hole substantially deeper, since 12% of recorded wells reach 600 feet or more. The deepest recorded well is 1,401 feet. Records show 13% under 100 feet, 39% from 100 to 300 feet, and 36% from 300 to 600 feet.

sections.heading: What Central wells typically produce
sections.html:
Among the Central-area records that report a pump yield, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces from 4.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute, which is a workable planning range for many household systems when the well, storage, pump, and fixtures are designed together.

Yield is not the same as available water in a house at every moment. A slower well may still serve a home with appropriate storage, while a stronger well does not remove the need for water-quality testing. The records show 2% under 1 gallon per minute, 26% from 1 to 5, 65% from 5 to 15, and 6% above 15. Most permitted use is domestic or household use.

sections.heading: Central water levels and the measurement record
sections.html:
The median static water level is 69 feet below the ground surface, with the middle half from 40 to 100 feet. That is the standing water level reported when measured, not the depth of the well and not necessarily the level while a pump is running.

Measurements by decade show 30 feet in the 1970s, 90 feet in the 2010s, and 60 feet in the 2020s. This does not establish a steady regional decline. The records are uneven, and the measured wells may not represent the same locations, elevations, or pumping conditions. Treat the figures as local context, then ask for the well’s original construction report and a current static-level measurement before relying on a water-supply assumption.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers around Central
sections.html:
Central has a long permit history, with records beginning in the 1950s and the newest permit year listed as 2025. The largest issuance periods were the 1970s with 556 permits and the 1990s with 541. The database includes 2,566 permitted wells, although only 1,677 are recorded as constructed and 1,660 report a total depth.

The most frequent driller names in these records are C. R. Smith Drilling, listed with 441 wells; C R Smith Drilling Inc, with 272; and James Drilling Company, with 129. These counts describe permit records, not current availability or a recommendation. For a new project, verify licensing, insurance, access requirements, estimated casing and grout, pump sizing, and what happens if the first drilling target is unproductive.

sections.heading: Planning a Central well drilling budget
sections.html:
The cost model for Central assumes fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss, at a drilling rate of $65 to $100 per foot. At the 277-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $18,000 to $27,700.

A functioning water system costs more than the hole. Including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, the modeled finished-well range is $24,000 to $39,700 at that median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, and site-specific electrical or trench work can change the bid. Ask every driller to separate footage, casing, development, testing, pump equipment, trenching, and electrical so competing proposals can be compared on the same scope.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying near Central
sections.html:
Low yield is not the only concern. The mapped area contains 15 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 3,617 historic mine features, and 17 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those locations do not prove a particular well is affected, but they justify testing and a careful review of the parcel’s distance and drainage relationship to old workings or cleanup areas.

Before buying, obtain the neighboring well permits, construction reports, yield information, and water-quality results. Confirm the proposed well location can maintain required separation from septic components and leave room for a replacement or repair. Ask the county and Colorado DWR about the permit and intended household use. Before building, have a driller evaluate rig access and a septic professional evaluate soils, slope, and the building envelope. Do not price the property on the median alone.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Central, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Central is 277 feet. The middle half of wells falls from 160 to 405 feet, while 12% reach 600 feet or more. The deepest recorded well is 1,401 feet. Fractured mountain bedrock makes individual results unpredictable, so nearby completed wells are useful when estimating a new drilling target.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Central, Colorado?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured granite and gneiss. At the 277-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at $18,000 to $27,700. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $24,000 to $39,700. Access, depth, and site conditions can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce near Central?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 4.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute. Records show 2% under 1 gallon per minute and 65% from 5 to 15. A yield test is specific to the well, and household performance also depends on storage and pump design.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Central, Colorado?
faq.a: Permit records do not establish that a particular well is safe to drink. The mapped area includes 15 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 3,617 historic mine features, and 17 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the actual well for appropriate contaminants, especially when the property is near mining or cleanup locations, and retest when conditions or ownership change.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping near Central, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded static water level was 30 feet below the surface in the 1970s, 90 feet in the 2010s, and 60 feet in the 2020s. That pattern does not prove a steady decline because the measurements may come from different wells and conditions. Get the subject well’s current static level and compare it with its construction record.
